Helicobacter Pylori Related Peptic Ulcer Disease

Helicobacter pylori is a ubiquitous organism that is present in about 50% of the global population. Chronic infection with H pylori causes atrophic and even metaplastic changes in the stomach, and it has a known association with peptic ulcer disease. The most common route of H pylori infection is either oral-to-oral or fecal-to-oral contact.

H. pylori treatment failure is defined as the positive stool antigen test or urease breath test 5 weeks after the last dose of eradication therapy. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) should be performed after (two) treatment failures. This is associated with higher eradication rates compared with individuals without AST. After treatment failure, the treatment should be individualized following the culture and sensitivity of the gastric biopsy or PCR.

Non-Pharmacological Management of functional dyspepsia (FD) focuses on dietary adjustments, lifestyle modifications, and stress reduction to alleviate symptoms like epigastric pain, burning, and early satiety. Key strategies include eating smaller, frequent meals, reducing fat and caffeine intake, avoiding trigger foods (spicy, acidic), and utilizing stress-reduction techniques like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), yoga, or meditation.

blocks.text: PUD caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or NSAID use is the most common cause of nonvariceal UGI bleeding. Characteristic findings are hematemesis, melena, or (infrequently) bright-red blood per rectum or a high serum BUN/creatinine ratio. Slow and/or chronic bleeding is suggested by iron deficiency and is typical of erosive disease, tumor, esophageal ulcer, portal hypertensive gastropathy, Cameron lesion (erosions found within large hiatal hernias), and angiodysplasia.

Obscure GI bleeding is recurrent blood loss without an identified source of bleeding despite upper endoscopy and colonoscopy. Patients aged ≤50 years are more likely to have tumors (leiomyomas, carcinoid, adenocarcinoma, or lymphoma), Dieulafoylesion, or Crohn’s disease. Older patients are more likely to have vascular lesions, such as angiodysplasia. Angiodysplasia is the most common cause of obscure GI bleeding overall (40% of all cases). Patients may present with either melena or hematochezia or positive fecal occult blood test (FOBT). The first step is to repeat upper endoscopy and/or colonoscopy, which is diagnostic in approximately 40% of cases.
